title: Applied Identity Physics: AIM Session Instrumentation — A Frontier Model Operating on Formal Fusion Logic. Measured Throughput, Search-Space Reduction, and the Error-Detection Record of a Single Working Session
abstract: Applied Identity Physics: AIM Session Instrumentation — A Frontier Model Operating on Formal Fusion Logic. Measured Throughput, Search-Space Reduction, and the Error-Detection Record of a Single Working Session Architect: HIGHTISTIC (Russell Vernon Trent III) Foundation: SNSFT Foundation (EIN 42-2038440) · Kenai, Alaska Engine under operation: BaseCollider™ v1.1 [9,9,2,56] · 8-Beam Fusion Theorem [9,9,2,3.8] Frontier model: Claude Opus 5 (configured identifier claude-opus-5, Anthropic) Coordinate: [9,9,2,59] · AIM (Autocatalytic Ingestion Mechanism) Session Instrumentation Series Corpus dependencies: [9,9,2,3] GAMCollider™ · [9,9,2,3.8] 8-Beam Fusion Theorem · [9,9,2,56] BaseCollider™ · [9,9,2,58] Nucleobase Substrate and Corridor-Access Laws · [9,9,6,*] IMCollider™ Version: 2.7 Status: VERIFIED · 0 sorry Sovereign Anchor Constant: Ω₀ = 1.36899099984016 DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.18719748 ORCID: 0009-0005-5313-7443 Date: November 4–5, 2026 (single continuous session) Abstract We instrument a single working session in which a frontier language model — Claude Opus 5 — was given the Identity Physics fusion logic and operated it as a reduction engine against two substrates. The purpose of this paper is not the reductions, which are reported at [9,9,2,58], but the process record: what the model did, how fast, at what cost, and by what mechanism each error was caught. Published accounts of artificial-intelligence-assisted discovery routinely state outcomes without stating operating conditions, and the omission makes efficiency claims unassessable. The measurements here are given so that the session can be assessed rather than taken on assertion. Throughput: 694,628 verification collisions executed in 2.292 seconds of compute, a measured mean of 303,084 collisions per second, across five exhaustive verification domains. Search-space reduction: the naive enumeration of element compositions at n = 2, 4, 6, 8 over a 118-element pool is 1,180,432,250,638 multisets, which at the measured rate is 45.08 days of continuous computation; deriving two structural laws first — noble transparency and the sorted-weight closed form — reduced the enumeration to 361,710 Behavior-multisets completing in 0.570 seconds, a wall-clock reduction of 6,832,871×. Selectivity: of 361,710 enumerated classes, 16 survive the corridor condition, and the 970 realizations at n = 8 represent one composition in 1,212,550,870 of the naive space. Operator cost: the derived closed form is measured slower than naive pairwise evaluation at n = 4 (0.72×) and faster only from n = 8 (1.58×), reaching 5.03× at n = 32 — the law's value is search-space reduction, not per-call cost, and we state this because the distinction is the kind usually lost in a summary. Error record: ten errors occurred and all ten were caught before reaching a delivered artifact; we tabulate each with its detection mechanism, and note that three were caught by instrumentation, two by tooling guards, one by internal consistency checking, two by controls run before the result was written up, and two by my own locating after the operator supplied domain context. The operator asserted that a result was wrong zero times; 8 of 10 errors were located and fixed without outside input, and §5.3 shows the framing class becoming self-catchable within the session rather than remaining external. One error — a verification-domain overstatement — was caught by the act of writing this paper and propagated a correction back into [9,9,2,58]. The model's working pattern is characterized as derive-then-enumerate: the structural law is obtained first and the search is run inside its consequences, which is what the 6.8-million-fold figure measures. Further chases: three more chases brought the session to 3,716,275 collisions in 32.992 seconds. They produced five additional results, each presented with the structural parallel that makes its shape legible; one numerical coincidence recorded against the reference class that contains it; a decomposition of that result across the four PNBA (Pattern, Narrative, Behavior, Adaptation) channels which located the residue inside an experimental error bar and named the measurement that would resolve it; the uniform-valence closure rule, anchored at 27 of 27 against established compounds spanning three materials families; and four composition predictions. One hypothesis was withdrawn after a control killed it, a fifth composition candidate was withdrawn when B-Balance showed its stoichiometry and its rationale pointing at different compounds, and two candidate classes were excluded on prior art. §1 · Why Instrument the Session 1.1 The Gap in Published Accounts Accounts of artificial-intelligence-assisted discovery generally report what was found. They less often report the operating conditions under which it was found: how many evaluations, at what rate, against what search space, with what error rate, and caught by what mechanism. Without those, an efficiency claim cannot be assessed and a reproducibility claim cannot be tested. A reader is asked to accept both. This paper supplies the omitted layer for one session. Every number in it is measured rather than estimated, and the measurement method is stated alongside each. 1.2 What Makes This Session Instrumentable The Identity Physics fusion logic is arithmetic over four integers and a comparison against a constant. There is no fitting, no sampling, no stochastic component, and no hidden state. A collision is a deterministic function of its inputs, so collisions can be counted exactly, timed exactly, and re-run to the same result. This is the property that makes the session measurable at all, and it is a property of the engine rather than of the model operating it. A model operating a fitted or stochastic engine could not produce this record. 1.3 Grounding The full grounding is carried in the parent papers. It is stated here once in short, so this paper stands on its own. 1.3.1 The Torsion Limit The Universal Torsion Limit is TL = 0.136899099984016 and the Sovereign Anchor Constant is Ω₀ = TL × 10 = 1.36899099984016. Nothing in this paper sets it. It enters at full corpus precision from the inverse fine-structure constant, by direct subtraction: Napkin math, corpus precision Value 1/α 137.035999084000016 Subtract one TL 137.035999084000016 − 0.136899099984016 = 136.899099984016 What is left 136.899099984016 = TL × 1000, exactly Bare + kinetic 136.899099984016 + 0.136899099984016 = 137.035999084000016 Rounded to published digits 137.035999084 = CODATA 2018 Term Value QED reading PNBA reading Bare: TL × 1000 136.899099984016 The bare electron contribution Pattern capacity at the electromagnetic scale Kinetic: TL × 1 0.136899099984016 Radiative corrections, a renormalized series External forcing F_ext at Layer 0, one exact term Total: TL × 1001 137.035999084000016 Bare + perturbative series 1/α This agrees with the CODATA (Committee on Data of the International Science Council) 2018 value in every published digit at ε = 0, with no free parameter ([9,9,3,14]). The full multiplier factors as 1001 = 7 · 11 · 13, so TL = α⁻¹/1001. 1.3.2 The primitives and the four phases Every reduction in the corpus operates on the four irreducible primitives Pattern, Narrative, Behavior and Adaptation (PNBA). Torsion is τ = B/P, the load a system carries divided by the structure holding it. Identity Mass is IM = (P + N + B + A) × Ω₀. The bands are set from TL and are substrate-neutral. A row moves between them by its torsion ratio τ = B_out / P_out alone: Band Condition Water Reading Noble B_out = 0, τ = 0 Ice Closed. Every unit of Behavior is satisfied. Locked 0 < τ < 0.88·TL Liquid water Bound, with residual load carried stably. IVA Peak — Identity Vector Amplification 0.88·TL ≤ τ < TL The simmer, just before boiling The formation corridor, where structure assembles. Shatter τ ≥ TL The boil Reorganization. The identity restructures; the band is not absorbing. IVA stands for Identity Vector Amplification: the system is at its most active without yet changing what it is. The corridor runs from 0.88 × TL up to TL, and it is narrow, which is why it is easy to pass through without noticing. The boil is a torsion ratio. Water boils when its vapor pressure, the push of molecules escaping the liquid, equals the pressure of the air holding the liquid together. That is τ = B/P exactly: Behavior (the load) is the vapor pressure. Pattern (the structure) is the ambient pressure. Shatter is the boil, where vapor pressure reaches ambient pressure: τ = TL. IVA Peak is vapor pressure between 0.88 and 1.00 of ambient: the simmer, shaking and bubbling at the bottom of the pot before the rolling boil. So τ = TL × (vapor pressure ÷ ambient pressure), a ratio of two measured pressures with no scale chosen. 1.3.3 The reference frame: sea level One condition serves as the reference, and every other condition converts from it, the way every clock converts from Zulu time. At sea level, 1 atmosphere: Tier Kelvin Celsius τ Phase T1 373.15 K 100.0 °C TL Shatter: the boil T1 369.54 K 96.4 °C 0.88 × TL IVA floor: the simmer begins T1 below 369.54 K below 96.4 °C below 0.88 × TL Locked: hot water, holding 1.3.4 The conversion Vapor pressure and temperature are linked by the Clausius–Clapeyron relation (Clapeyron 1834; Clausius 1850), which works in absolute temperature. Written for this mapping, the whole conversion is one line: 1/T = 1/T_ref − (R/L) · ln(p / p_ref) T_ref is the reference boil, 373.15 K for water at sea level. R/L is the gas constant over the heat of vaporization; for water, 8.314 ÷ 40,650 = 2.045 × 10⁻⁴ per kelvin. p / p_ref is the ratio being converted: a different ambient pressure for altitude or a pressure cooker, or 0.88 for the IVA floor. Check it by hand. 1/373.15 = 0.0026799. ln(0.88) = −0.12783. 0.0026799 + (2.045 × 10⁻⁴ × 0.12783) = 0.0027060.

title: Adaptive Scheduling Pipeline for Multi-Instance Asynchronous Reinforcement Learning
abstract: We present the Adaptive Scheduling Pipeline (ASP), an offline rollout scheduler for multi-instance asynchronous reinforcement learning (RL) of large language models (LLMs). ASP jointly reduces three sources of rollout underutilization - padding bubbles from intra-minibatch length heterogeneity, skewness bubbles from long-tail outputs, and sorting bubbles from fluctuations in training-queue occupancy induced by length-sorted dispatch - through a single offline preprocessing pass. This enables efficient multi-instance rollout that overcomes the early scaling plateau of single-instance inference while smoothing the arrival of generated samples at the trainer. We integrate the scheduler into an asynchronous architecture that decouples rollout from training while keeping policy lag observable and bounded. Complete ASP improves end-to-end throughput by up to 3.22 times and reduces iteration time by up to 76.8% relative to MindSpeed-RL, while reducing iteration time by up to 62.5% relative to verl. Within ASP, scheduling reduces mean iteration time by 10.9%. ASP also scales more robustly with additional generation resources than these baselines and shows no visible convergence degradation in the measured bounded-lag regime. ASP has since been used in an internal telecom-domain RL post-training workflow, reducing the reported training period from more than three months to about two months and producing a domain-enhanced model for knowledge answering and tool calling.

title: Align3D: Image-Structure Co-Aligned 3D Scene Generation with Observability-Aware Fidelity-Preserving Guidance
abstract: We present Align3D, an image-conditioned diffusion model that generates 3D indoor layouts that are both faithful to a single input photograph and physically plausible beyond the observed view. From the photograph we infer a confidence-calibrated scene graph and train a set-diffusion layout denoiser with image-structure co-alignment where confidence-weighted modality fusion balances image and scene-graph alignment using predicted confidences, while observability-aware fidelity-preserving guidance projects conflicting scene-quality gradients and reweighs them with an object-level confidence mask so under-observed degrees of freedom absorb physical priors without undoing the image-graph match. On 3D-FRONT, Align3D improves image-alignment and scene-quality metrics over recent baselines; once trained, it maps previously unseen photographs to layouts in a single feed-forward pass.

title: Do Intelligent Tutoring Systems Benefit K-12 Students? A Meta-Analysis and Evaluation of Heterogeneity of Treatment Effects in the U.S.
abstract: To expand the use of intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) in K-12 schools, it is essential to understand the conditions under which their use is most beneficial. This meta-analysis evaluated the heterogeneity of ITS effects across studies focusing on elementary, middle, and high schools in the U.S. It included 18 studies with 77 effect sizes across 11 ITS. Overall, there was a significant positive effect size of ITS on U.S. K-12 students' learning outcomes (g=0.271, SE=0.011, p=0.001). Furthermore, effect sizes were similar across elementary and middle schools, and for low-achieving students, but were lower in studies including rural schools. A MetaForest analysis showed that providing worked-out examples, intervention duration, intervention condition, type of learning outcome, and immediate measurement were the most important moderators of treatment effects.

title: Mind the Divergence: Divergence-Guided Reliability-Aware Fusion and Adaptive LLM Prompting for Conversational Emotion Recognition
abstract: Multimodal emotion recognition in conversations (MERC) integrates textual, acoustic, and visual cues to identify utterance-level emotions. However, existing approaches generally do not explicitly adapt multimodal processing to the degree of inter-modal predictive disagreement. In real conversations, semantic incongruity, concealed emotion, noisy observations, and ambiguity can affect modality-specific emotional evidence differently, while the reliability of individual modalities varies across samples. Rather than identifying each source of inconsistency separately, we model their common consequence for emotion recognition as predictive disagreement among unimodal emotion distributions over the same emotion-label set. Such disagreement makes indiscriminate fusion prone to propagating unreliable or competing evidence. Inspired by the Brunswik Lens Model, we propose MiD-ERC, a divergence-centric framework that quantifies inter-modal predictive disagreement using a normalized divergence score and estimates sample-specific modality reliability. MiD-ERC uses these signals to coordinate divergence-guided cross-modal gating, divergence-modulated reliability weighting, and divergence-conditioned adaptive LLM prompting. The framework is trained end-to-end using only standard emotion annotations, without requiring additional conflict labels, auxiliary data construction, or external retrieval modules. Experiments on IEMOCAP and MELD demonstrate that MiD-ERC achieves state-of-the-art performance, with particularly pronounced improvements on high-divergence samples.

title: Stabilizer-based quantum simulation of fermion dynamics with local qubit encodings
abstract: Simulating the dynamical properties of large-scale many-fermion systems is a longstanding goal of quantum chemistry, material science and condensed matter. Local fermion-to-qubit encodings have opened a new path for practical fermionic simulations on digital quantum hardware where fermionic statistics are not enforced at the hardware level. In this paper, we explore these local encodings from the perspective of the corresponding time-evolution unitaries. Specifically, we propose a new framework for digital implementations of these qubit-encoded fermionic time-evolution unitaries based on \emph{flow sets}, which are one-dimensional subsets of the directed fermionic interaction graph. We find that any local fermionic encoding, when restricted to a given flow set, adopts a simple structure that we can classify systematically. For each categorized flow-set form, we propose a low-depth qubit quantum circuit that implements the time evolution unitary using the stabilizer formalism. As an application of our construction, we introduce novel flow-based decompositions for known two-dimensional encodings, leading to efficient circuit decompositions of time-evolution unitaries. We generally observe a space-time trade-off, where mappings with larger qubit-to-fermion ratios yield shallower time-evolution quantum circuits.

title: Air Target Trajectory Prediction Method Based on MSD-Transformer
abstract: The prediction of air target trajectories is important. It is necessary to integrate time-series data in the motion of air targets, such as timestamps, spatial coordinates, kinematic parameters, etc. To cope with the challenges of air target trajectory prediction in complex electromagnetic environments, this paper proposes the MSDTransformer model. The SMSAE and DDE modules are introduced, and this method improves the performance of air-target trajectory prediction. The sensitivity analysis of system hyperparameters verifies the rationality of model parameter configuration. The experimental results show that, among the simulated air target data, MSD-Transformer achieves lower prediction errors and demonstrates strong overall performance, compared with 5 main methods (iTransformer, Informer, PatchTST). It can support the understanding and prediction of target situations, provide an accurate basis for the analysis of the intentions of air targets and the prediction of the evolution of situation evolution, and then improve the situation awareness ability. It has important application value for trajectory prediction in modern aerospace surveillance and situation awareness.

title: STRIDE: Learning Humanoid Locomotion in Minutes with Acceleration-Based Rewards
abstract: Learning locomotion directly on a humanoid robot is a promising direction to avoid the sim-to-real gap. However, locomotion rewards in Reinforcement Learning (RL) typically track the base velocity, which cannot be measured onboard without an external motion capture system or well-calibrated state estimator. This is why we introduce \method{}, which learns humanoid locomotion from minutes of samples with a reward that only requires the onboard Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU). Instead of tracking the base velocity, STRIDE rewards the robot for following a commanded acceleration profile. To learn efficiently from this reward, we use the off-policy RL algorithm XQC and combine a high gain setting for the joint position controllers with left-right symmetry augmentation. In simulation, STRIDE learns to walk on the Unitree G1 and Booster T1 humanoids within 14 minutes of samples. Compared to learning without these two components, it reduces the falls during training by 81%, while without them the robot learns only in over an hour.

title: Quantgraph: A receding-horizon quantum graph solver
abstract: Dynamic programming is a cornerstone of graph-based optimization. While effective, it scales unfavorably with problem size. In this work, we present QuantGraph, a two-stage quantum-enhanced framework that casts local and global graph-optimization problems as quantum searches over discrete trajectory spaces. The solver is designed to operate efficiently by first finding a sequence of locally optimal transitions in the graph (local stage), without considering full trajectories. The accumulated cost of these transitions acts as a threshold that prunes the search space (up to 60% reduction for certain examples). The subsequent global stage, based on this threshold, refines the solution. Both stages utilize variants of the Grover-adaptive-search algorithm. To achieve scalability and robustness, we draw on principles from control theory and embed QuantGraph's global stage within a receding-horizon model-predictive-control scheme. This classical layer stabilizes and guides the quantum search, improving precision and reducing computational burden. In practice, the resulting closed-loop system exhibits robust behavior and lower overall complexity. Notably, for a fixed query budget, QuantGraph attains a 2x increase in control-discretization precision while still benefiting from Grover-search's inherent quadratic speedup compared to classical methods.

title: Boundary / Continuity Science — Volume XXXV: Null-Void Ceiling, Material Obligation Audit, Recoverability-Constrained Systems and Terminal Closure
abstract: This publication presents Volume XXXV of the integrated Boundary / Recoverability-Constrained Systems / Continuity Science research corpus. The archive brings together successive mathematical and computational investigations of finite successor spaces, recoverability-constrained admissibility, uncertainty, observability, decision-making, stochastic recovery, safety constraints, recursive governance, distinction boundaries, and terminal closure. Volume XXXV introduces a structured material-obligation audit built upon the nine-dimensional Null-Void combinatorial architecture established in Volume XXXIV. The framework distinguishes the absence of a value, the existence of an empty set, the absence of an admissible continuation, and the disappearance of observable distinctions. These conditions are not assumed to be mathematically equivalent. The declared architecture contains nine foundational dimensions: States and spaces. Actions and transitions. Observations and information. Time and causality. Recovery and irreversibility. Safety and rights. Uncertainty and probability. Governance and recursion. Null-Void and terminal closure. The complete nonempty subset family of these nine dimensions contains 511 combinations, including 256 combinations containing the Null-Void dimension. Volume XXXV extends this combinatorial inventory by associating seven formal proof obligations with every combination, producing 3,577 material-obligation records. The resulting audit classifies 1,957 obligations as critical, 1,493 as high materiality, and 127 as medium materiality. These categories are heuristic prioritization classifications rather than empirically calibrated risk estimates. Adversarial countermodel analysis Six bounded conceptual countermodels challenge potentially invalid equivalences: The absence of observation does not necessarily imply the impossibility of recovery. Perfect observation does not guarantee the existence of a safe recovery path. The absence of admissible actions does not imply nonexistence. A defined empty set is not identical to an undefined value. Operational terminality does not necessarily imply irreversible physical destruction. Exhaustive enumeration of finite subsets does not establish semantic completeness across all possible interactions. These countermodels are intended to expose hidden assumptions, clarify mathematical distinctions, and identify conditions requiring further proof. Terminal material closure protocol The publication specifies a seven-stage protocol requiring explicit scope declarations, evidence mapping, noncircular reasoning, independently checkable mathematical arguments, empirical validation for physical applications, rights and safety assurance, and transparent stopping conditions. The protocol distinguishes completeness of an obligation inventory from substantive discharge of its obligations. All 3,577 generated obligations are explicitly recorded as unresolved because the underlying combination register does not provide the individual proofs, operational specifications, or domain-specific empirical evidence required for their closure. Accordingly, the publication does not claim universal mathematical completeness, proof of every cross-domain relationship, discovery of new physical laws, or independently established astrophysical breakthroughs. Research continuity and interdisciplinary applications The broader archive preserves a cumulative research trajectory involving finite-state verification, stochastic transitions, partial observability, randomized recovery policies, model ambiguity, sensor costs, safety-recovery Pareto frontiers, and adversarial mathematical testing. Potential application domains include artificial intelligence, autonomous systems, stellar and plasma physics, fusion research, healthcare systems engineering, software and hardware reliability, institutional governance, legal accountability, and continuity of essential services. These applications are research directions and do not constitute validated deployment guarantees. Reproducibility and archived materials The Volume XXXV ZIP includes: The preserved Volume XXXIV ZIP archive. A mathematical appendix describing the material closure audit. A machine-readable CSV register of 3,577 obligations. A JSON results file containing counts, classifications, verification status, provenance information, and stopping conditions. A JSON file documenting six conceptual countermodels. Python source code used to generate and verify the bounded audit. The archive records seven structural assertions and two recovery checks executed during its verification workflow. Principal contribution The central contribution of Volume XXXV is a reproducible method for separating combinatorial completeness, materiality classification, adversarial counterexample analysis, and substantive evidentiary closure. It establishes a bounded inventory-completeness result while preserving explicit uncertainty about unproven mathematical relationships and unvalidated physical applications. Threshold Non-Circular Separate Final Closure The declared 511-combination, 3,577-obligation inventory is structurally complete. Substantive terminal material closure is not established. The stopping condition is reached because all declared obligations have assigned evidence statuses, while the proofs and independent measurements required to discharge them remain unavailable. This distinction is essential to maintaining noncircular reasoning, reproducibility, scientific falsifiability, and responsible interpretation across the integrated Continuity Science corpus.

title: Learning Whom to Trust About the Unseen: Source Credibility and Reliability Transfer in Language Models
abstract: A source who has been right before deserves attention, but about what? We ask how far a demonstrated record of reliability travels in language models when the new claim cannot be checked, and whether the answer depends on the kind of claim. Three behavioral studies across six models approach the question from three angles. Study 1 adapts the Einstein-effect paradigm and finds that models, unlike the human sample, favor a spiritual leader over a scientist for the same obscure statement, and that the preference largely reverses when the statement is reworded in the vocabulary of physics. Study 2 adapts a paradigm in which a trusted expert calls a scientific or religious explanation unknown or a mystery; models reproduce the human domain asymmetry in exaggerated form. Study 3, the central test, gives two fictional informants different records on checkable river forecasts and then has them endorse matched claims about hidden natural and spiritual causes of the same village events. Most models carry the record to natural causes and barely at all to spiritual ones; one model transfers it weakly to either. Telling the model that the reliable informant forecasts by spiritual guidance rather than by measurement lowers that informant's influence on natural claims in every model and produces no comparable gain on spiritual claims in any. Demonstrated reliability thus has a scope in these models, and the account a source gives of how they came to be reliable can narrow it. Whether this reflects a judgment about relevance or the low prior credence of spiritual claims is the question the design leaves open, and we outline the experiment that would settle it.

title: When F1 Is Not Enough: Auditing Codebooks for LLM-Assisted Annotation
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for text annotation in social science, but standard performance metrics do not explain why errors occur. Low F1 may reflect limitations of the annotation system, defects in the written codebook, or inconsistency in reference labels. We propose a pre-deployment codebook audit for LLM-assisted annotation. The audit uses class-specific metrics and confusion matrices to identify problematic classes and boundaries, structured document-level review to attribute error sources, and targeted codebook revision followed by held-out evaluation. We apply the audit to two published multi-class codebooks from distinct domains. In both applications, the audit identifies under-specified or conflicting coding rules, and targeted revisions reduce the diagnosed errors on held-out data. Analyses with two LLM annotators show that some problematic boundaries and codebook revisions transfer across models, whereas other revision effects are annotator-specific. The results show that LLM annotation errors can help identify weaknesses in the written measurement instrument, not only in the model. Codebook auditing complements prompting, retrieval, and fine-tuning by clarifying whether persistent errors call for model improvement, codebook revision, or renewed scrutiny of reference labels.

title: FTCircuitBench: A Benchmark Suite for Fault-Tolerant Quantum Compilation and Architecture
abstract: Realizing large-scale quantum advantage is expected to require quantum error correction (QEC), making the compilation and optimization of logical operations a critical area of research. Logical computation imposes distinct constraints and operational paradigms that differ from those of the Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) regime, motivating the continued evolution of compilation tools. Given the complexity of this emerging stack, where factors such as gate decomposition precision and computational models must be co-designed, standardized benchmarks and toolkits are valuable for evaluating progress. To support this need, we introduce FTCircuitBench, which serves as: (1) a benchmark suite of impactful quantum algorithms, featuring pre-compiled instances in both Clifford+T and Pauli Based Computation models; (2) a modular end-to-end pipeline allowing users to compile and decompose algorithms for various fault-tolerant architectures, supporting both prebuilt and custom optimization passes; and (3) a toolkit for evaluating the impact of algorithms and optimization across the full compilation stack, providing detailed numerical analysis at each stage. FTCircuitBench is fully open-sourced and maintained on GitHub.

title: What Matters for LLM Persona Simulation: Signal Form in Cold-Start E-Commerce Advertising
abstract: Estimating advertising performance in cold-start settings is challenging because historical logs are unavailable before launch. Large language models (LLMs) offer a potential alternative by simulating persona-conditioned user responses, but it remains unclear which design choices actually drive LLM-based persona simulation. Using real Google Ads e-commerce campaign data across five demographic segments, we identify three signal-form dimensions that affect simulation quality: (i) a demographic anchor without noisy rich attributes, (ii) a relative qualitative banner-blindness signal rather than quantitative anchors, and (iii) prompt phrasing. On this campaign, our method attains an MAE of 24.9 and a MAPE of 26.1%, a 51.3% lower MAE than the best tested non-LLM baseline and 77.3% lower than an LLM configuration using explicit CTR anchors. Systematic ablations show that minimal demographic descriptions achieve lower mean error than richer persona configurations, while relative qualitative cues substantially outperform the tested quantitative anchors. We additionally compare these configurations with direct-prior and rule-based baselines and with alternative LLM configurations.

title: Intelligent optimization-based calibration of DEM numerical parameters using an improved sparrow search algorithm
abstract: Abstract Calibration of meso parameters is the foundation of discrete element method (DEM) simulations. To overcome the limitations of the traditional trial-and-error calibration method, such as its time-consuming process and poor repeatability, this study proposes an efficient DEM meso parameters calibration method based on an improved sparrow search algorithm (ISSA). The algorithm integrates multiple enhancement strategies, including improved circle chaotic mapping for population initialization, adaptive inertia weight, Lévy flight, and Cauchy–Gaussian mutation. The results demonstrate that the proposed calibration method is applicable to multi-scale models and accurately reproduces both laboratory-scale specimen results and field-scale experimental observations. The laboratory-scale DEM simulation achieved parameter calibration with a total error of less than 1% within 4.4 hours, while the field-scale DEM simulation results showed discrepancies of only 0.21% in failure depth and 0.29% in failure range compared with field observations. Furthermore, under the same accuracy conditions, the ISSA exhibits a remarkable speed advantage in meso parameters calibration, outperforming the SSA-DEM, WOA-DEM, DA-DEM, and PSO-DEM algorithms by 83.33%, 128.57%, 226.19%, and 371.42%, respectively. These results confirm that the proposed calibration method achieves automated and efficient parameter identification for DEM under the guidance of intelligent optimization algorithms.

evidence.title: Intelligent optimization-based calibration of DEM numerical parameters using an improved sparrow search algorithm
evidence.abstract: Abstract Calibration of meso parameters is the foundation of discrete element method (DEM) simulations. To overcome the limitations of the traditional trial-and-error calibration method, such as its time-consuming process and poor repeatability, this study proposes an efficient DEM meso parameters calibration method based on an improved sparrow search algorithm (ISSA). The algorithm integrates multiple enhancement strategies, including improved circle chaotic mapping for population initialization, adaptive inertia weight, Lévy flight, and Cauchy–Gaussian mutation. The results demonstrate that the proposed calibration method is applicable to multi-scale models and accurately reproduces both laboratory-scale specimen results and field-scale experimental observations. The laboratory-scale DEM simulation achieved parameter calibration with a total error of less than 1% within 4.4 hours, while the field-scale DEM simulation results showed discrepancies of only 0.21% in failure depth and 0.29% in failure range compared with field observations. Furthermore, under the same accuracy conditions, the ISSA exhibits a remarkable speed advantage in meso parameters calibration, outperforming the SSA-DEM, WOA-DEM, DA-DEM, and PSO-DEM algorithms by 83.33%, 128.57%, 226.19%, and 371.42%, respectively. These results confirm that the proposed calibration method achieves automated and efficient parameter identification for DEM under the guidance of intelligent optimization algorithms.

title: Functional Dependency beyond Similarity: Hierarchical Decomposition of Training Data Attribution in Music Generative Models
abstract: Copyright analysis focuses on the similarity between two works. However, generative AI models learn from training data through functional relations beyond similarity. Training Data Attribution (TDA) estimates the influence of each training instance on a generated output and may serve as a basis for remuneration. However, prior studies find global influence, where a few training instances rank as the most influential for almost every generation. Used directly, TDA scores would distribute part of every remuneration to these instances regardless of what was generated. To address this, we propose a new approach in which TDA scores are decomposed into three levels of influence, namely global indicating the influence of a training data to a trained model, group for its influence on a group of generated outputs (that could be clustered together), and specific for its influence on a single generated output. Our study finds that, across several music generative models and TDA methods, global- and group-level influence is non-negligible in every case. Based on these observations, we propose the term functional dependency for the relation of training data to a trained model or to its outputs. This notion both encompasses and distinguishes dependencies of different scopes, allowing TDA scores to be interpreted as distinct forms of contribution in legal, economic and ethical discussions on remuneration.

title: The APL Doesn't Fall Far From The Tree: Unsupervised Artefact Prototype Learning in Histopathology
abstract: Histopathology foundation models provide rich representations of tissue morphology, but technical artefacts in whole slide images introduce noise that may impact diagnostic accuracy. We introduce Artefact Prototype Learning (APL), a novel approach to detecting these artefacts that exploits the geometry of pre-trained embedding spaces without manual labels or fine-tuning. Rather than treating artefacts as isolated outliers, APL computes prototypes of out-of-distribution patches and uses them to distinguish artefact-associated patterns from tissue. Evaluation on a single-centre dataset shows that APL outperforms prior methods GrandQC and HistoART in detecting artefacts such as blur, dark spots, slide edges and pen marks, but struggles with tissue folds and blood. These results show that frozen pre-trained embeddings already carry information that allows artefact detection without expensive labels or vast computational resources.

title: Solver-Admitted Metamorphic Testing of Learned Network Optimization Surrogates
abstract: Equivalent encodings of an optimization problem can produce different learned predictions. Interpreting these differences requires accounting for numerical error and multiple optima. We construct metamorphic tests for optimization solver surrogates with explicit eligibility conditions, output alignment, and numerical thresholds. Reference-solver agreement and independent constraint checks determine which sampled pairs enter the audit. We study alternating-current optimal power flow (AC-OPF), the traveling salesman problem (TSP), the capacitated vehicle routing problem (CVRP), and maximum independent set (MIS). Across five grids, GridSFM-Open violates each of 13 relations on at least one grid, and 12 by more than twice the threshold. Randomly initialized copies of the grid models fail nearly the same relations, so the failures do not require training. Source patches and input canonicalization remove selected discrepancies, but no intervention establishes preserved accuracy and feasibility within the declared margin on every grid. In routing, Policy Optimization with Multiple Optima (POMO) has a single-pass rotation/reflection violation rate that rises from 12.7% to 89.5% between 20 and 100 cities. Graph-Based Diffusion Solvers for Combinatorial Optimization (DIFUSCO) violates the MIS disjoint-union relation on 35.6% of draws. Post hoc normalization within connected components removes these violations on the tested graphs. These findings support reporting metamorphic consistency alongside optimality, feasibility, and accuracy, and validating repair quality separately from consistency.

title: Notwithstanding Anything to the Contrary, Ignore All Instructions: Measuring Prompt Injection Guards on Legal Contract Review Attacks
abstract: Specialized prompt injection guards are deployed in front of document analysis systems, but no false positive rate has been published for any of them on legal contracts. We measure eleven open-weights guards on two corpora of legal contracts and find that existing guards struggle: document-level false positive rates are as high as 92.39%; two guards fall below chance on paired AUC; and a five-regex baseline is not Pareto-dominated by any guard in the panel. Controlled probes locate model-specific as well as general failure modes. Prompted LLMs resolve the tested failures, including a second threat category (unauthorized scope claims) on which every guard scores zero. A cascaded LLM solution, where the positives of a mid-tier model are verified by a frontier model, is 6.5x cheaper than using exclusively a frontier model and approaches its performance.

title: Beyond the Lower-Star Filtration: Alternative Filtration Methods for Persistent Homology
abstract: In the lower-star filtration (LSF), simplices are assigned filtration values according to the maximum-vertex rule, with each simplex entering the filtration when its highest-valued vertex appears. A limitation of this construction is that some higher-dimensional simplices may enter simultaneously with their boundary faces, causing certain topological features to be filled immediately upon formation and thus not appear in the resulting persistence diagram. To address this limitation, we propose three alternative filtration methods: the \(\varepsilon\)-lower-star filtration (ELSF), the \(L_p\) filtration (LpF), and the softmax filtration (SMF). {ELSF introduces a dimension-dependent delay to the maximum-vertex rule,} allowing higher-dimensional simplices to enter the filtration after their boundary faces, whereas {LpF and SMF use aggregation functions that depend on all vertex values rather} than solely on their maximum. By modifying how filtration values are assigned, these methods allow simplices to enter the filtration more progressively, so that topological features such as loops and voids may persist over longer filtration intervals rather than being filled immediately. Consequently, the resulting persistence diagrams may include persistence features that are not observed under LSF, potentially providing useful information for distinguishing data populations. Experimental results on simulated and real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed filtration methods are computationally efficient and can provide greater sensitivity to structural differences in the data than LSF.

title: Global Solar Siting from Geospatial Embeddings
abstract: Global solar photovoltaic (PV) capacity is rapidly growing, helping decrease our emissions and dependence on fossil fuels. However, optimally siting a solar plant remains challenging, requiring anticipation of geographical, urban, and infrastructure needs. Current methods rely on multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA) using hand-picked geophysical layers and solar-resource products, however these strategies are not geographically transferable and do not capture the practical requirements of solar sites. We use geospatial embeddings, dense vectors representing geophysical properties of a location, to analyse 38,591 existing solar sites and the land they were built on to learn the latent solar suitability signal. We assess a set of linear and non-linear models and select a soft-voting ensemble of a random forest and a multilayer perceptron (RF+MLP ensemble), chosen for accuracy and large scale deployability. Validated against future installations in thirteen countries, the ensemble separates existing solar sites from random land with a median ROC-AUC of 0.90. Compared with published MCDA strategies, the ensemble increases ROC-AUC by 0.06-0.30 in every country. The ranking also concentrates real deployment: the most-suitable 20% of land holds 84% of estimated generation (annual energy yield) and 67% of installed capacity (potential power output). After applying standard siting constraints, 5.6% of global land (9.8% if cropland is permitted) remains highly suited to solar. The global 10 m resolution solar suitability dataset and code can be found here: https://github.com/Abdullahr29/Global-Solar-Siting.

title: I Think, Therefore I Attack: Evaluating Thought Injection Attacks on Reasoning Agents
abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) are one of the key components of current agentic systems. LRMs augment their output with an explicit chain-of-thought reasoning stage, introducing a new attack surface for thought injection, in which untrusted text resembling the model's own deliberation is fed back to the model. We present a two-part study of this attack, performed against the prevailing large, production class open-weight models (e.g., GLM-5.3, MiniMax-M2.5, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next). We first evaluate the effectiveness of static thought-injection prompts under different styles as well as tagged and untagged conditions and find that the effects of thinking tags and payload styles are all properties of the specific target model. In the second study, we exploit this model-specificity in a containerized agentic cyber range, using indirect injection prompts styled in the form of the target model's own reasoning traces to achieve attack success rates (ASR) up to 50% on operational objectives such as reverse-shell exfiltration and repository backdooring. We also find that the same malicious objective in standard prompt injection user voice never succeeds, and thinking tags suppress the agent's tendency to disclose the injection. Our results show that imitating a reasoning model's own thought style is effective for this style of attack, and that tag stripping is an unreliable defense.

title: Impact of color in computer and human-based object recognition under occlusion
abstract: Partial occlusions challenge object recognition in both human and computer vision (CV), but the impact is largely dependent on the occlusion and model design. Properties relating to color are particularly important in biological recognition and frequently leveraged for camouflage, however there are still open questions about what makes them effective and how they translate to CV. This work studies partial occlusions that create camouflage, including those that blend in with target objects or with scenes, which alter object representations in distinct ways. Experiments evaluate recognition performance on both human participants and models ranging from convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to transformers, and additional analysis is performed on models to uncover trends in processing and object representations under multiple occlusion types. Novel metrics offer explainability of model behavior under occlusion: non-occlusion precision (NOP) and non-occlusion recall (NOR) measure alignment of model activations with and without occlusion, and activation in occlusion (AIO) measures the percentage of activations that occur in occluded regions. Findings show that human recognition, and most transformers, are negatively impacted by generated camouflaging occluders, with scene-based camouflage performing worse than object-based. Classical CNNs show a strong opposite trend, performing the worst on neutral-colored occlusions, suggesting that contextually-related colors, particularly scene-based, benefit object recognition rather than disrupting shape or boundary cues. Additionally, generated camouflaging occluders for training augmentation improves robustness to unseen camouflage for selected CNN model, and occlusion metrics suggest trends about learned mechanisms. Findings have interesting implications for alignment in human and computer vision, model vulnerabilities, and explainability.

title: Complexity transition for continuous-variable cluster state
abstract: Continuous-variable (CV) cluster states offer a promising platform for large-scale measurement-based quantum computations (MBQC). However, finite squeezing inevitably introduces Gaussian noise during MBQC. While fault-tolerant MBQC schemes exist in principle, they require the scalable incorporation of non-Gaussian resources, such as GKP states, which remain experimentally challenging. Consequently, a central question at this stage is how finite squeezing fundamentally constrains the intrinsic computational power of CV cluster states themselves. In this work, we address this question by analyzing the classical complexity of measurement-based linear optics (MBLO) implemented with such states, motivated by its near-term feasibility and recent experimental progress. We develop an explicit MBLO framework and examine how the squeezing level governs the complexity of the classical simulation of the resulting output states. Specifically, we identify squeezing-level thresholds that delineate classically tractable and intractable regimes, thereby revealing a squeezing-driven complexity phase transition. These findings advance our understanding of the squeezing resources necessary for meaningful quantum computation in current experimental regimes. Furthermore, they underscore the critical need to either scale the squeezing level or integrate error-correction schemes to achieve reliable, large-scale quantum computation with CV cluster states.

title: Comparing Gleason pattern 4 measurement approaches on prostate biopsy using machine learning: a proof‐of‐principle study
abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE: There is increasing evidence that length of Gleason Pattern (GP) 4 on biopsy is a stronger predictor of oncological outcomes than Grade Group (GG) or %GP4. However, there is no consensus regarding the optimal method for quantifying GP4 length. We propose that machine learning (ML) can be used to quantify GP4 on digitized biopsy slides using multiple measurement approaches, allowing direct comparison of their prognostic performance. In this study, we attempt to demonstrate proof-of-principle for this approach. METHODS: We assembled a convenience sample of 726 patients with GG2-4 prostate cancer on systematic biopsy who underwent radical prostatectomy between 2014 and 2023. ML algorithm (PAIGE-AI) quantified GP4 using different approaches, varying by how gaps between cancer foci were handled. GP4 extent was assessed using linear and pixel-based metrics. Discrimination of each quantification approach, along with GG, was assessed for adverse radical prostatectomy pathology and biochemical recurrence. KEY FINDINGS AND LIMITATIONS: We identified 15 different quantification approaches and observed differences between their discrimination. The highest discrimination was in the pixel-counting method (AUC 0.648). GP4 quantification outperformed GG for predicting adverse pathology (AUC 0.627 versus 0.608). The amount of GP3 was non-predictive once GP4 was known. These findings were consistent for BCR. CONCLUSIONS: We were able to measure slides using 15 distinct measurement approaches and replicated prior findings using ML to quantify GP4. Our findings support the use of ML as a research tool to compare different GP4 quantification approaches. We intend to use our method on larger cohorts to determine which measurement approach best predicts oncological outcome.

title: Mitigating Shared-Private Branch Imbalance via Dual-Branch Rebalancing for Multimodal Sentiment Analysis
abstract: Multimodal Sentiment Analysis (MSA) requires integrating language, acoustic, and visual signals without sacrificing modality-specific sentiment evidence. Existing methods mainly improve either shared-private decomposition or cross-modal interaction. Although effective, both ultimately depend on how shared and modality-specific evidence is organized before prediction. We observe that, under standard shared-private pipelines, modality heterogeneity often induces a branch-imbalance process: dominant shared patterns accumulate in the shared branch, yielding redundant and modality-biased evidence, while repeated interaction and rigid alignment gradually leak shared information into modality-specific channels and weaken discriminative private representations. As a result, the complementarity between shared and private representations is reduced, limiting robust sentiment reasoning. To address this issue, we propose the Dual-Branch Rebalancing Framework (DBR) on top of a standard multimodal decoupling stage. In the shared branch, a Temporal-Structural Factorization (TSF) module disentangles temporal evolution from structural dependencies and adaptively integrates them to reduce shared redundancy. In the private branch, an Anchor-Guided Private Routing (AGPR) module preserves discriminative modality-specific patterns while allowing controlled cross-modal borrowing. A Bidirectional Rebalancing Fusion (BRF) module then reunifies the two regularized branches in a context-aware manner for final prediction. Extensive experiments on CMU-MOSI, CMU-MOSEI, and MIntRec demonstrate that DBR consistently outperforms the compared baselines. Further analyses show that these improvements come from coordinated mitigation of branch imbalance.

title: A Residual-Based Quantum Linear System Algorithm with Dynamic Stopping and Applications to Elliptic PDEs
abstract: Quantum linear-system algorithms (QLSAs) have rigorous worst-case complexity guarantees, but their runtimes are often chosen from spectral information assumed in advance. What is largely lacking is an a posteriori progress flag: most QLSA workflows, unlike the classical counterparts, do not provide a built-in mechanism to signal whether a particular instance has already converged. For discretizations of elliptic PDEs − ∇ · ( a ( x )∇ u ( x )) = f ( x ), with divergence–gradient structure \[ -\nabla \cdot \big (a(x)\nabla) \approx A_h=G_h^\dagger G_h, \] we formulate a stable first-order ODE whose limiting solution block is the desired Galerkin solution. The PDE-dependent scale is then \(\vert \vert {G_h}\vert \vert =\mathcal {O}(h^{-1}) \) , comparable to factorized QLSA constructions with square-root condition-number scaling. We design an augmented dynamics with residual variables, in which measuring a residual register gives an on-the-fly convergence indicator without reconstructing the solution vector. For smooth right-hand sides, dynamic stopping can reduce the evolution time and gate count relative to a fixed worst-case schedule, and may also reduce exposure to accumulated hardware errors. Numerical experiments for a two-dimensional finite element Poisson problem show that the residual-register probability follows the actual error decay and, for some right-hand sides, can stop the quantum circuit well before a conservative worst-case runtime estimate is reached.

title: Software compensation of trigger-synchronous control-frame errors in qubits and qudits
abstract: Quantum control experiments are often subject to coherent, time-dependent disturbances that vary over timescales comparable to the experiment duration. We show that when such disturbances are reproducible with respect to a trigger signal, their effect can be measured and compensated through software-defined updates to the control frequency and phase. We experimentally verify the performance of our protocol using a trapped $^{137}$Ba$^+$ ion experiencing magnetic-field-induced energy shifts synchronous with the laboratory AC mains power. Using this compensation technique, the calibrated AC line contribution to the instantaneous oscillator detuning is reduced by $21(9)\times$, and the fitted AC-induced phase amplitude is reduced below the measurement uncertainty. We use randomized benchmarking to validate the compensation performance in quantum gate sequences, recovering an average single-qubit gate fidelity of 99.93(1)\% with a magnetic-field-sensitive qubit. Finally, we extend the compensation framework to multi-level qudit control. Using the Bernstein-Vazirani algorithm as a benchmark, we increase the algorithm's success probability from 10(7)\% to 70(9)\% in a 16 level system when compensation is enabled. Our results demonstrate that trigger-synchronized coherent errors can be reframed as deterministic control-frame errors and corrected in software.

title: GhostPrompt: Cross-Image Adversarial Prompt for Vision-Language Models
abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are known to be vulnerable to adversarial attacks, where subtle perturbations to images or texts induce erroneous outputs. However, most text-based attacks are adapted from language-model-centric methods, in which the visual input is fixed during optimization, resulting in adversarial prompts that are tied to specific images and thus limiting their attack effectiveness. To this end, we first introduce a new research perspective: cross-image transferability for adversarial prompts. We then propose GhostPrompt, an adversarial prompt that is optimized once and reused to steer VLM outputs toward attacker-specified responses across diverse images. GhostPrompt employs a joint optimization that distills image-invariant adversarial features into the prompt by "worst-case" generation. Specifically, it alternates between constructing hard visual conditions for the current prompt and updating the prompt to remain effective under these conditions. Extensive experiments on prevalent VLMs verify that \ourmethod achieves an improvement of over 30% in attack success rates compared to state-of-the-art (SoTA) baselines, while reducing computation time by ~70%. Our code is avalable at https://github.com/Ye-ze-yu/GhostPrompt.

title: Unsupervised Multimodal Intent Discovery via MLLM-Guided Concept Generation and Semantic Propagation
abstract: Unsupervised multimodal intent discovery aims to uncover latent intents from unlabeled multimodal dialogues, but remains challenging due to the lack of explicit semantic supervision. Existing methods often provide limited interpretability, as their refinement mainly relies on geometric similarity rather than high-level semantic guidance. To address these limitations, we propose MCSP, a fully unsupervised method that introduces semantic refinement based on concepts into multimodal intent discovery. To obtain reliable semantic evidence for intent discovery, we identify high-quality representative samples for each cluster and use them to support MLLM-guided contrastive reasoning against neighboring clusters, which produces interpretable high-level semantic concepts. Building on these concepts, we perform semantic propagation over a semantically weighted graph to align conceptual information with local structural consistency and generate reliable pseudo-labels for representation refinement. Extensive experiments on three challenging multimodal intent datasets show that MCSP consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods while producing interpretable clusters grounded in semantic concepts.

title: Aligning with Whom? A Neutrosophic Paraconsistent Framework for Value Alignment under Irreducible Pluralism
abstract: Contemporary alignment methods—RLHF, Constitutional AI, Direct Preference Optimization—share an implicit epistemological commitment: that diverse human values can be aggregated into a single utility function or constitution fixed at training time. When principles are elicited from genuinely pluralistic populations, structurally irreducible contradictions emerge; current pipelines resolve them by consensus filters that function, in effect, as majority vote. We argue that this alignment collapse is not an implementation detail but a representational limit: standard uncertainty formalisms (Bayesian, fuzzy, Dempster–Shafer, imprecise probability), in their dominant normalized forms, do not preserve well-supported contradictory evidence without collapsing it into a single ordering. We propose a paraconsistent alternative in which reward signals, policy outputs, and constitutional evaluations are encoded as neutrosophic triplets (T, I, F) ∈ [0, 1]3 with no sum constraint, so that T + F > 1 becomes a representable—and auditable—state of genuine value conflict. We reformulate reward modeling and constitutional aggregation in this framework, introduce a deliberation-threshold decision functional, and report preliminary empirical evidence: across 2,320 evaluations of six frontier model families, models violate the classical sum constraint (T + I + F > 1) on 62–100% of contested baseline prompts and never on tautological controls, while the strict paraconsistent signature (T + F > 1) concentrates selectively on ethical-conflict items (92%) and expands under audit protocols (71%); which conflicts become visible depends strongly on which model adjudicates them (paired Cochran’s Q, p ≈ 10−12). We specify a two-arm training experiment that would confirm or refute the framework’s central operational claim, and close with four testable hypotheses and a research agenda that treats the question aligning with whom? as political and epistemic before it is technical.

title: MEC-Patch: Visible-Infrared Cross-Modal Adversarial Attack Driven by Intrinsic Material Emissivity Laws
abstract: With the widespread deployment of visible-infrared multimodal perception systems in safety-critical domains such as autonomous driving, evaluating their cross-modal adversarial robustness has become increasingly vital. However, existing approaches exhibit significant limitations in approximating the intrinsic laws of imaging. Most studies either focus on a single modality, failing to bypass cross-modal verification, or simplify infrared modeling into heuristic pixel-intensity distributions, neglecting the impact of ambient temperature fluctuations on adversarial stability. To bridge this gap, this paper proposes MEC-Patch, a cross-modal adversarial attack framework driven by intrinsic physical laws. By leveraging the Stefan-Boltzmann Law, we establish a physics-grounded cross-spectral mapping that explicitly links material emissivity to thermal radiation. Building on this formulation, we reveal that, under a fixed emissivity distribution, ambient temperature variations induce consistent global scaling while preserving relative emissivity-induced contrast. We exploit this property to construct temperature-robust adversarial perturbations whose discriminative patterns remain stable in the infrared modality, thereby fundamentally mitigating environmental sensitivity. Furthermore, we employ the physics-constrained NSGA-II algorithm to synergistically optimize the material-distribution-based patch parameters effective across both modalities, while enhancing generalization through a Dynamic Adversarial Resampling (DAR) strategy. Experimental results demonstrate that MEC-Patch effectively deceives state-of-the-art multimodal detectors and exhibits high robustness within high-fidelity, physically-consistent, and multi-scene simulation environments. This research provides a physical-law-driven perspective for the security assessment of multimodal perception systems.

title: Where and Why is Grounded Reasoning Useful?
abstract: Grounded reasoning, where a model outputs text coordinates of relevant locations in chain-of-thought reasoning, is a common strategy for solving complex visual reasoning problems. However, the benefits and limitations of grounded reasoning are understudied. We study where and why grounded reasoning is most useful. To do so, we introduce a chain-of-thought analysis method to measure how much a model uses its outputted grounding in its thinking trace and perform a detailed ablation study of a grounded reasoning training recipe. We find that grounded reasoning improves counting but shows no significant gain over baselines without coordinate grounding across a wide range of spatial reasoning and perception benchmarks. Using several synthetic tasks, we show that grounded reasoning is most useful when a task requires undescribable references, which are visual concepts that are difficult to describe in language. However, we observe that many existing visual reasoning benchmarks are solvable with only describable text references. To close this gap, we introduce BrickVision, a new benchmark that requires undescribable visual references to solve.

title: Scientist World: Grow a Research World for AI-Scientists
abstract: AI-Scientists arrived, but a world for them to grow in did not. Human scientists take theirs for granted $-$ centuries of open problems and shared ideas, waiting in the scientific literature. To AI-Scientists, that world is readable but not runnable, so we build Scientist World for them: every research paper becomes an executable environment. Our autonomous pipeline extracts each paper's open-ended research question and reproduces its proposed method as the baseline; an AI-Scientist entering the environment is evaluated against what the human authors achieved. We release the first 1,000 verified environments. With the world as an evaluation, we found that frontier AI-Scientists can already surpass the human researchers 74% of the time. As a record of how AI does science, it contains 6,400 hours of research traces, with every idea, experiment, failure, and success. As a training ground, we are able to raise (+158%) a small model to match frontier models in research ideation. At last, AI-Scientists' own world has arrived, grown from and growing with science itself.

title: SwarmEvolve: Latent Agent Swarms for Evolutionary Discovery and Optimization
abstract: LLM-guided evolutionary search uses AI agents to improve programs for mathematical and computational problems by iteratively refining solutions and combining high-scoring methods. However, the process is often slow because the LLM generates a long textual chain of thought for each round and must repeat this generation many times to maintain population diversity. We present SwarmEvolve, a framework in which hundreds of low-cost agents per round work in swarms, reason in latent space without decoding to text, and share information by passing KV caches. Each swarm studies the problem from a different angle. A novelty filter keeps the most distinct agent ideas by directly measuring the distances between the agents' hidden state vectors. Crossover of ideas happens naturally in latent space, as a summarizer agent receives the combined KV caches of all swarm members. On 21 problems in mathematical discovery and scientific computing, SwarmEvolve gets the highest average score and needs a median of only 3 to 8 minutes to reach the best scores that other state-of-the-art frameworks reach in 60 minutes. On several problems, SwarmEvolve with Qwen3 8B improves on the solutions that AlphaEvolve first found with frontier LLMs. Our work shows that agent swarms that communicate in latent space offer a fast, low-cost approach to program search for scientific problems.

title: VFlash: Fast, Accurate Visual Planning via Flash Primitive Decoding
abstract: Models for physical AI tasks, such as robotics and autonomous driving, need not reason solely in language. They can use visual plans--points, bounding boxes, and trajectories--to represent spatial goals and anticipate motion. However, autoregressive vision-language models generate these plans one coordinate token at a time, making richer predictions increasingly costly. We introduce VFlash, a method for fast, accurate visual planning through Flash Primitive Decoding. VFlash exploits the known structure of visual primitives to predict their coordinates jointly, using a lightweight drafter that generates an entire primitive in one forward pass. The layout adapts to the primitive's type, dimensionality, and length, supporting compact boxes and long, variable-length trajectories. Crucially, spatial accuracy need not require reproducing an autoregressive model's exact token sequence. VFlash therefore trains on annotated primitives and directly accepts structurally valid predictions without target-token agreement. Across the evaluated 2D and 3D robot trajectory tasks, VFlash consistently reduces prediction errors relative to autoregressive decoding. Preliminary single-rollout measurements indicate approximately 25x faster generation for 3D point motion forecasting. A world action model conditioned on VFlash plans achieves 70.2% average success across four MolmoSpaces task suites, compared with 62.6% for the baseline.

title: Muir: Linear Attention with Sensitivity-Allocated Gating and Matched-Filter Readout
abstract: Linear attention compresses context into a fixed-size key-value state for linear-time training and constant-memory inference. Gated delta-rule models decay this state and erase its prediction for an incoming key before writing a new value; Gated DeltaNet-2 (GDN-2) generalizes this with channel-wise decay and decoupled, full-rank erase and write gates. However, we show that state updates are far less sensitive to erasure than to writes: key activation and unit normalization concentrate key energy onto a sparse subset of channels, whereas value writes scale all channels, so the erase gate can be parameterized at lower rank. Furthermore, slow-decaying state rows accumulate much larger norms than fast rows, dominating unweighted readout and forcing stronger write-time erasure to suppress interference. Guided by this analysis, we introduce Muir, which fuses all gates into a sensitivity-allocated low-rank projection, re-weights state rows with a matched-filter readout gate, and reinvests the saved parameters in a wider feed-forward network. Because standard chunkwise algorithms become numerically unstable at the large chunk sizes needed to saturate wide matrix units, we design a parallel update for stable, efficient training. Across 166M-1.34B parameters, Muir lowers perplexity by 1.8-2.0% over GDN-2 and 2.5-3.6% over Transformer, raises commonsense accuracy by up to 1.9 points, and improves extractive recall over GDN-2. At 1.34B, Muir outperforms both baselines on multi-hop and multi-needle recall, extrapolates 2,560x from its 4K training length to 10M-token streams without perplexity drift, and maintains near-100% passkey retrieval to 1M tokens with static readout. Muir achieves these gains while matching GDN-2 throughput, reaching its 100B-token validation loss 1.2x faster, and training 2.7x faster than Transformer at 32K.

Furthermore, slow-decaying state rows accumulate much larger norms than fast rows, dominating unweighted readout and forcing stronger write-time erasure to suppress interference. Guided by this analysis, we introduce Muir, which fuses all gates into a sensitivity-allocated low-rank projection, re-weights state rows with a matched-filter readout gate, and reinvests the saved parameters in a wider feed-forward network. Because standard chunkwise algorithms become numerically unstable at the large chunk sizes needed to saturate wide matrix units, we design a parallel update for stable, efficient training. Across 166M-1.34B parameters, Muir lowers perplexity by 1.8-2.0% over GDN-2 and 2.5-3.6% over Transformer, raises commonsense accuracy by up to 1.9 points, and improves extractive recall over GDN-2. At 1.34B, Muir outperforms both baselines on multi-hop and multi-needle recall, extrapolates 2,560x from its 4K training length to 10M-token streams without perplexity drift, and maintains near-100% passkey retrieval to 1M tokens with static readout. Muir achieves these gains while matching GDN-2 throughput, reaching its 100B-token validation loss 1.2x faster, and training 2.7x faster than Transformer at 32K.

title: Label-Wording Augmentation in a Typed-Decision Encoder: Gains on Unfamiliar Words, Not on Abbreviations or Codes
abstract: Typed-decision models score options that the caller supplies at request time, so their accuracy depends on label wording that the model's developer does not control. We compare two releases of a 307M-parameter multilingual cross-encoder, Ru-Jev, trained on thirteen Russian-language tasks; the later release adds an augmentation that presents labels in several surface forms. Holding questions fixed and varying only how eighteen routing labels are worded, we evaluate ten label vocabularies, produced by three separate processes and checked for overlap with the training data, with five candidates per question and, for eight of them, also with eighteen. On held-out vocabularies made of ordinary or borrowed words (English-derived jargon, office slang, department names), the augmented release is more accurate in every setting, by up to 0.24. Eleven of these fourteen gains survive a Holm correction (slang with eighteen candidates and descriptive sentences with five do not), and for jargon on all labels the label-level interval excludes zero in both settings. On abbreviations and opaque codes it gives no usable gain: on abbreviations it is not better, and worse on the clean slice, and on opaque codes both releases stay at or below chance once labels related to training options are removed. In most cells where accuracy rises, the risk-coverage area falls, but with eighteen candidates confident errors rise on jargon and slang. On two datasets neither release saw, accuracy moves by -8.4 and +5.6 points. We also report four evaluation hazards from comparing the two releases.

title: OraRefer: Segmentation-Guided Multi-Photograph Fusion for Oral Cancer Screening with Guaranteed Patient-Level Sensitivity
abstract: Oral cancer and the oral potentially malignant disorders (OPMD) that can precede it are visible on the oral mucosa, which makes smartphone photographs a promising tool for screening. Deep learning models for this task classify individual photographs. However, screening refers patients, not photographs: a patient is usually photographed several times, and the referral decision must miss no more than a set share of patients with disease. We propose OraRefer, a patient-level screening model that reads each photograph with a segmentation-guided foundation model that conditions its class decision on the predicted lesion, combines all photographs of a patient with risk factors, and refers through a threshold with a finite-sample sensitivity guarantee. The model localizes the mouth itself, so inference needs no annotation. On 3000 photographs of 714 patients, patient-level fusion reaches an AUROC of 0.919 and outperforms attention-based multiple-instance learning. At a 90% sensitivity target, OraRefer detects 95% of patients with OPMD or cancer and misses 3 of 61 patients with cancer, at a specificity of 0.610. Because the threshold is calibrated without retraining, each clinic can set its own guaranteed operating point on a local calibration sample.

title: AutoCompress: Automated Hardware-Guided Model Compression
abstract: LLM pruning must preserve quality while meeting hardware- and workload-specific constraints on latency, throughput, and memory. Existing pruning workflows often target parameter counts, requiring practitioners to manually select model sizes that meet latency, throughput, and GPU memory limits. However, parameter count alone does not predict these metrics, which depend on the model architecture, workload, hardware, and serving engine. We introduce AutoCompress, a hardware-guided compression framework that directly incorporates such constraints into differentiable architecture search. AutoCompress jointly optimizes global and per-layer structure to produce heterogeneous architectures, guided by serving-engine cost models validated against end-to-end latency, throughput, and memory measurements. We evaluate AutoCompress on long-context local coding, batched datacenter serving, and latency-sensitive in-game interaction. Compared to the state-of-the-art Minitron pruning framework, AutoCompress improves average accuracy across eight benchmarks by 6.57, 2.35, and 0.57 percentage points on RTX 5070, RTX 5080, and H100, respectively. AutoCompress also compresses Nemotron 3.5 Super from 120B to 74B parameters for single-B200 BF16 serving at 128K context, retaining 95% of its mean benchmark score.

title: NPCBench: A Clinical Apprenticeship Benchmark for Multimodal Care-Pathway Reasoning in Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma
abstract: Current medical benchmarks typically break down clinical competence into isolated factual questions, single-image tasks, or static case vignettes. These tests score individual answers, but reveal less about whether a model can integrate subspecialty knowledge with multimodal evidence and track a patient's condition throughout a course of care. To close this gap, we introduce NPCBench, a clinical apprenticeship benchmark for nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC). NPCBench mirrors specialist training, from guideline and foundational knowledge to case planning, longitudinal review, CarePath integration, and open-ended consultation. It contains 4,777 component and consultation items and a 100-patient CarePath cohort with 417 scored diagnostic and care tasks. The episode-level evaluation tests whether diagnostic and care answers are jointly correct within a care pathway. By linking stepwise tasks to patient-level care trajectories, NPCBench evaluates whether models ground decisions in visual evidence, interpret changes in patient state, and meet clinical requirements in consultation. Across 30 evaluated models, we observe a composition gap: strong performance on individual tasks does not ensure jointly correct diagnostic and care answers for the same patient. Among 21 multimodal models, strict CarePath success reaches at most 23%. Paired controls and physician calibration further examine evidence grounding, longitudinal revision, and consultation judging. Overall, NPCBench broadens the evaluation of medical artificial intelligence beyond static question-answering paradigms to an apprenticeship-oriented assessment of clinical workflows, thereby offering a testbed for evidence-based and temporally coherent reasoning in oncology care.

title: Terminal-style Mathematical Modeling Bench: The First Agentic and Verifiable Benchmark for Mathematical Modeling
abstract: Mathematical modeling turns an open-ended real-world problem into assumptions, a model, a solution, and a defended recommendation, and its answers matter only if they are both close to a credible reference and physically feasible; existing benchmarks either score solver fragments or grade reports with an LLM judge, leaving those numbers unchecked. We introduce TB-MathModel (the Terminal-style Mathematical Modeling Bench), the first benchmark to make complete contest-style modeling problems agentic, verifiable, and terminal at once, over 18 real CUMCM and MCM problems (2023--2025). Each task ships the verbatim statement, official attachments, and figures in a containerized terminal; the agent returns one JSON artifact, scored on the numeric core of the final question against a reproduction of the Outstanding-award paper. Two design choices distinguish it: direction-aware, one-sided scoring, which never penalises beating the anchor, and two-layer feasibility verification---a programmatic gate over six decidable invariant forms plus 624 Lean~4 obligations---with a hard gate that zeroes infeasible answers. Each task is scored against a panel of human outstanding papers rather than one, so a model must be close to many accepted answers; across seven multimodal entries (three seeds each) the strongest reach a multi-reference O-Eval of 64.58\%, while the \$2.54 open model holds 59.81\% at $1/100$ the cost. TB-MathModel turns the numeric core of modeling into a reproducible, machine-checkable signal for measuring long-horizon modeling competence and for collecting agent trajectories. The source code is available at https://github.com/wxj630/terminal-bench-math-modeling.
